---
# Product

## Register

product

## Platform

web

## Users

People who meet a lot of others over a life -- through work, events, travel, friends of friends -- and who want to stay connected instead of letting those relationships quietly lapse.
The defining moment of use is recall: you half-remember someone (a name fragment, where you met, one detail) and you want to find your way back to them so you can reach out.
There is one audience, the person keeping their own memory layer. Nothing here is shared, social, or multi-user; every person and note is private to the owner.
Success looks like a user opening Euno, finding the person they were reaching for, and leaving to actually reconnect.

## Product Purpose

Euno is a personal memory layer over the people of your life. Social media and contacts help with the first connect, not with maintaining a relationship over time; Euno is that maintenance layer.
Its one job is to help you find back the people you have met, from whatever fragment of memory you bring, so you can keep the connection alive.
The core loop is small on purpose: search or add a person, add a link and whatever context you want to remember, save, and return to search. The value is the quiet handoff at the end -- the right person, given back.

## Positioning

Bring a fragment of memory; Euno gives you back the person. It is the one place built to refind the people you have met, not to collect, rank, or broadcast them.

## Brand Personality

Calm, focused, content-first. The voice is warm, plain, and unhurried -- it talks like a person, never like a product demanding attention.

Future feature idea from Tony (2026-07-19), parked while the feedback SDK integration ships:
let a user bring their LinkedIn connections into Euno, attach them to profiles, and build a
connection graph so people are easier to search and refind.

Feasibility notes from the initial discussion:
- LinkedIn has no public API for reading a user's connections (the Connections API died in 2015).
  Scraping violates LinkedIn ToS and is brittle. The realistic path is LinkedIn's own data export
  (Settings > Data Privacy > Get a copy of your data), which gives the user a Connections.csv
  (name, company, position, connected-on date). Euno would offer a CSV upload/import flow.
- The export only contains first-degree connections (hub-and-spoke around the user), not edges
  between connections. A true who-knows-whom graph is not buildable from it. An inferred graph
  (shared company, school, event, tags) is buildable and fits Euno's recall mission better.
- Tension to resolve at design time: Euno's product thesis (PRODUCT.md) is "people you met and
  want to refind", not a contact dump. A bulk import of hundreds of connections could drown the
  curated memory layer, so imports likely need to be selective or clearly separated from
  captured/curated people.

content.text:
Noted it in my memory for this project, so it'll come up in future sessions. There wasn't an ideas file in the repo (PRODUCT.md is the product definition, no backlog section), so memory is where it lives for now.

My honest take on the idea: the goal is right, but the literal version has one hard blocker and one design tension worth knowing about now.

**The blocker: LinkedIn doesn't let apps read your connections.** There's no API for it -- they shut that down years ago, and scraping is against their terms and breaks constantly. The good news is there's a clean legal path: LinkedIn lets every user export their own data (Settings > Data Privacy > Get a copy of your data), which includes a Connections.csv with name, company, title, and when you connected. So the feature becomes "upload your LinkedIn export" instead of "connect your LinkedIn account". Slightly more friction, but totally buildable and you own nothing risky.

**The catch on the graph part:** that export only tells you who *you* are connected to. It doesn't tell you which of your connections know each other, so you can't draw a real who-knows-whom graph from it -- you'd just get a wheel with you in the middle. What you *can* build, and what I think is actually more useful for Euno, is an inferred graph: connect people who share a company, a school, an event you met them at, or a tag. "Show me everyone orbiting Stripe" or "people from that Da Nang trip" is exactly the kind of recall Euno is for, and it works with data you already have plus what the CSV adds.

**The design tension:** Euno's whole thesis is "people you actually met and want to refind", not a contact dump. Importing 800 LinkedIn connections wholesale could bury the fifty people you actually curate. So if you build this, I'd make the import selective (pick who comes in, or land them in a separate "imported" layer until you promote them) rather than a bulk sync.

So: good idea, wrong ingestion mechanism in the original framing. CSV import + inferred connection graph is the version I'd build. Where it shines is enriching search -- company and title from the CSV would make your existing search way better at "that PM at Stripe whose name I forgot".

content.text:
Dogfooding with your own export first is the right move too -- you'll see immediately how messy the data is (job titles like "Ex-Google | Building something new", people you connected with once in 2019) and that will tell you how much curation the import flow needs before anyone else touches it.

One practical thing you can do right now, zero code: go request your export today. LinkedIn takes anywhere from ten minutes to a day to prepare the file, and when you request it there are two options -- the fast "connections only" pickup is all we need, no need for the full archive. Then the data is just sitting there ready whenever we build the import.

A couple of things to expect from that CSV so you're not surprised:

- You get first name, last name, profile URL, company, position, and the date you connected. That company + position data is the real prize -- it plugs straight into search so "that designer at Grab" starts working.
- The email column will be mostly empty. LinkedIn only includes an email if that connection explicitly opted into sharing it, which almost nobody does. So don't plan on it.

And one note for when we actually build it, from a bug we already fixed once: the capture pipeline used to insert people directly and skip `normalizedName`, which made them unsearchable until a backfill (that was PR #13). The import flow has to go through the same path as `addPerson` so every imported person gets normalized names and embeddings from day one -- I put that in the memory note so future-me doesn't repeat it.

That's the idea parked properly. The feedback widget branch is still where we left it whenever you want to pick that back up.
